item.title: Hon Hai posts record July revenue
item.description: Taipei, Aug. 5 (CNA) Hon Hai Precision Industry Co. posted record unaudited consolidated revenue of NT$946.512 billion (US$29.27 billion) in July, marking the first time the company's monthly revenue has exceeded NT$900 billion and representing a 54.19 percent increase from a year earlier, the company announced Wednesday.

item.title: Navy Relieves Commander of Sub USS West Virginia
item.description: Cmdr. Joseph Sammur was relieved as the commanding officer of USS West Virginia (SSBN-736) (Blue Crew) last week due to a loss of confidence, the Navy announced Saturday. Sammur’s relief follows an investigation into a maintenance issue, a Submarine Forces Public Affairs spokesperson told USNI News on Monday. West Virginia is currently in port for maintenance, according to the Navy’s Saturday news release. Cmdr. Luke Kelvington, Submarine Squadron 20 deputy for training, has temporarily assumed command of West Virginia’s Blue Crew. Sammur, who assumed command nearly a year ago on Aug. 14, 2025, has been temporarily reassigned to Submarine Group

item.title: Female bomber kills at least three, injures 21 near Moscow restaurant, authorities say
item.description:
MOSCOW — A homemade bomb carried by a woman killed at least three people and injured 21 near an upscale restaurant in central Moscow on Saturday evening, authorities said, amid unconfirmed speculation on social media that the attack may have been linked to the war in Ukraine. The explosion occurred just before 8 p.m. close to an Italian restaurant located in one of Moscow’s seven Stalin-era skyscrapers at Kudrinskaya Square, the police said. Russia’s National Anti-Terrorism Committee (NAK) said an unidentified woman carrying an improvised explosive device had tried to get into the restaurant but had been stopped by a security guard.

The post Female bomber kills at least three, injures 21 near Moscow restaurant, authorities say appeared first on Hawaii Tribune-Herald.

item.title: Obituaries for August 2
item.description:
Bella Barbieto Bautista, 83, of Hilo died July 6 at Hilo Benioff Medical Center. Born in the Philippines, she was an interpreter for the State of Hawaii, a member of the Church of Latter-day Saints Ponahawai and she enjoyed gardening and had a love of flowers, with orchids being her favorite. Visitation from 9-10:15 a.m. on Saturday (Aug. 8) at the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Ponahawai with funeral service at 10:30 a.m. Burial to follow at Alae Cemetery (Sec. L Row L Plot 8). Flowers are welcomed. Survived by daughter, Jonalyn (Andrew) Scott of Mililani; sons, Jessie (Rachel) Bautista and Junel (Crizeth) Bautista; brother, Joseph (Anita) Barbieto and numerous grandchildren and great-grandchildren. Arrangements by Dodo Mortuary, Inc.

The post Obituaries for August 2 appeared first on Hawaii Tribune-Herald.

item.title: Trump says he will hold off on fresh Iran attack in hope of quick deal
item.description:
CAIRO — U.S. President Donald Trump said late on Saturday he would hold off on a fresh attack on Iran as long as a deal could be reached quickly to halt Iran’s nuclear ambitions and reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Iran and “other Middle Eastern Countries” asked for a time to complete a deal that would lead to “the Immediate, Complete and Total” reopening of the Strait and “an end to Iran’s nuclear threat,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform. “Based on this request, I have agreed, for the future benefit of the WORLD and, likewise, the survival of a successful and prosperous Iran, to cancel the attack, subject to being able to rapidly make a DEAL.” Israel “joins me in this commitment,” Trump wrote. Israel did not immediately make a public statement on the issue. Iran warned the U.S. this weekend against any “adventurous action” and said it would retaliate decisively if American forces followed through on Trump’s threats of fresh attacks on Iranian targets. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi’s comments in separate phone calls on Saturday with senior Turkish, Pakistani and Saudi officials came just hours after Kuwait’s army said it destroyed hostile drones launched by Iran against several vital facilities.

The post Trump says he will hold off on fresh Iran attack in hope of quick deal appeared first on Hawaii Tribune-Herald.

item.title: Europe’s crazy rich royals and their lavish retreats
item.description:
The royal families of the past — like those of the present — were fond of their countryside getaways. These lavish retreats provided an escape from the city and the summer heat, a place for diversions like hunting and horseback riding, and enough land to build grand showpiece palaces and gardens. While Europe has many royal summer palaces you can visit, a few are remarkable for their sheer size, over-the-top opulence, and the larger-than-life personalities who built them.

item.title: Do you still have Crown Lynn memories in your house?
item.description:
Source: RNZ Pacific

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — In the 1970’s, a small retail store — Ho-Ching Annesley, Inc. — in American Samoa — sold foodstuffs, but was well-known locally for selling affordable plates, bowls, cups & saucers. The Crown Lynn pottery was brought in by the company from New Zealand, in a container over the following years, as ‘seconds’ — meaning they did not make the mark to be sold by Crown Lynn Potteries, Ltd. due to a variety of imperfections during kiln firing. However, they were sold by as miscellaneous sales; and, they found a perfect market in American Samoa at the time.

When a container came in, the word would go out, and crowds of women of all ages would be seen sitting in front of the shelves that held the pottery, on the floor, cross-legged — hand sorting, mix matching their choices for their household plates, bowls, cups & saucers.

At the time of the Crown Lynn factory’s closure, a third of the workforce was from Samoa, according to the Te Toi Aku - Crown Lynn & Clay Museum that reopened the last brickworks kiln in Auckland, NZ recently, with a display space for ceramic and pottery artists.

The museum’s director Louise Stevenson told Culture 101/ RNZ- Life and Culture, that each handle and rim of Crown Lynn cups looks slightly different. “It makes you think about the fact that every single crown and cup that was made, we’ve identified, would have had 14 pairs of hands involved in the process of making.”

For American Samoa, Samoa News notes to this day, some local households still have remnants of their mother’s or grandmother’s collection of dishes that are pieces that hold memories of eating meals, and sharing food with your family and friends. [photo: RNZ/ Braydon Priest]

item.title: First American Samoa resident earns UH online social work degree
item.description:
By 
University of Hawaii News

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — When Vivian Legaloimoe Ho Ching was named first runner-up in the 2026 Miss American Samoa contest, she added another remarkable achievement to a journey already defined by service, leadership and dedication to her community.

A recent graduate of the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa’s Thompson School of Social Work & Public Health, Ho Ching is the first student to complete the Master of Social Work (MSW) online program while residing in American Samoa. Her accomplishment highlights the importance of creating pathways that allow students to pursue advanced degrees while remaining in their home communities.

“Vivian represents the very best of what is possible when educational opportunity, cultural identity and community service come together,” said Theresa Kreif, director of Pacific Partnerships and Workforce Development Initiatives. “Her success demonstrates that students can pursue advanced education while remaining connected to their families and cultural values.”

“Increasing access to our online social work programs allows students throughout the Pacific to pursue a high-quality education without having to leave the communities they plan to serve,” said Meripa Godinet, associate dean of the Thompson School. “Vivian’s achievement demonstrates how accessible educational pathways can prepare local professionals, strengthen the regional social service workforce, and create lasting benefits for families and communities. Her accomplishment also honors the social work alumni connected to American Samoa who came before her, whose service, leadership, and commitment helped establish a strong foundation for future generations of social workers.”

A COMMITMENT TO SERVICE

For Ho Ching, both her education and her pageant role are grounded in a commitment to service. While completing her MSW field internship at the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs clinic in American Samoa, she provided support to veterans and their families, developing skills grounded in Pacific values.

“My journey has always been about giving back to the community that has shaped me,” said Ho Ching. “Earning my MSW while remaining in American Samoa allowed me to stay connected to my culture and grow as a professional.”

As first runner-up in the Miss American Samoa contest, Ho Ching serves as a cultural ambassador, advocating for issues important to Pacific communities. Her social work background reinforces this role, emphasizing advocacy, social justice, and community wellbeing.

“I see both social work and the pageant experience as opportunities to uplift others,” she said. “Both are rooted in listening to people and working to create positive change.”

Ho Ching’s success reflects the Thompson School’s broader commitment to strengthening the social service workforce throughout the Pacific. Her achievement serves as a model for future students, proving that advanced education can be pursued without leaving home, while bridging the gap between professional expertise and cultural stewardship.

item.title: Father of Georgia school shooter sentenced to 15 years in prison
item.description:
A man who gave his troubled son the rifle he used to kill four people at a Georgia high school was sentenced on Thursday to 15 years in prison, the culmination of the state’s first case in which a parent was convicted of second-degree murder for a mass shooting committed by his child. Colt Gray, 16, was sentenced to life in prison without parole on Tuesday for the 2024 school shooting by a Barrow County Superior Court judge. Two days later, the same judge sentenced his 55-year-old father, Colin Gray, to far less than the 80 years prosecutors had requested.

The post Father of Georgia school shooter sentenced to 15 years in prison appeared first on Hawaii Tribune-Herald.

item.title: Are social media algorithms killing Pacific news? (Part 2)
item.description:
That is the trap. Pacific publishers depend on Meta to reach their audiences. Meta can change the way it distributes their work without warning, cut their reach without explanation and leave them with nowhere meaningful to appeal.
Better internet will help connect the Pacific. It will not solve the problem of one foreign company controlling so much of the region's news distribution.
item.source:markdown:

item.title: Are social media algorithms killing Pacific news? (Part 1)

item.title: UPDATE: Aircraft incident at Fitiuta Airport
item.description:
Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — Port Administration American Samoa (PAAS) is providing an update regarding the runway excursion on Tuesday, July 28, 2026 involving Samoa Airways Twin Otter (5W-FAY) Flight 990, at Fitiuta Airport, Manu’a Islands.

The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) has completed its initial assessment and has officially released the aircraft from its investigative hold. PAAS will continue its investigation of the runway excursion today and tomorrow. PAAS will also coordinate with Samoa Airways on the next steps for the removal and recovery of the aircraft.

The runway is open with normal flight operations, with two Samoa Airways flights operating today. A Samoa Airways engineer is now onsite. The flight advisory remains in effect while recovery operations are coordinated.

As previously announced, due to the unavailability of a chartered aircraft today, PAAS has arranged for a charter flight today — Thursday July 30th — to continue its onsite investigation. Port Director Barney Sene and members of the Airport investigation team will travel to Fitiuta to assess the incident site, coordinate recovery operations with Samoa Airways, and the safe restoration of the affected area.

The aircraft and the immediate surrounding area continue to be secured by PAAS while recovery plans are finalized.

PAAS appreciates the continued support and cooperation of all partner agencies involved in the response. Additional information will be released as it becomes available.

item.title: Lewis Wolman: Nov 20, 1957 — Jul 25, 2026
item.description:
Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — Lewis Joel Wolman passed away peacefully at home in Boulder, Colorado, on Saturday, July 25, 2026, with his family by his side.

Lewis was born November 20, 1957, in Madison, Wisconsin, to Joseph "Murphy" Martin Wolman and Anne Wolman. The youngest of 5 siblings, he grew up around the newspaper business, which instilled a curiosity and passion for the news, public issues, reading, community, service, and lifting people and places.

He graduated from West High School in Madison in 1974 at 17 years old. After one year of school at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, he headed out west to the University of California, Santa Cruz, where he graduated with a degree in Environmental Planning.

He eventually got a job as a Program Officer in the U.S. Office of Coastal Management, which took him to American Samoa, where he would spend the better part of the next 40 years.

In American Samoa, he built a wonderful life and career. He met his wife, Eletise Matagi, raised four children (Tavie, Jessica, Homer, Iopa), and held many leadership positions in both the private and public sectors.

He was perhaps most recognizable for his work as the publisher and editor of the Samoa News for 20 years, where he worked tirelessly to keep the people informed of the issues that mattered most to the people of American Samoa.

His career after Samoa News included, but was not limited to, Country Manager of Bluesky Communications, CEO of ASTCA, President of the American Samoa Chamber of Commerce, CEO of the GHC Reid Group, and Special Advisor to the Governor of American Samoa. He loved to work.

While his work kept him busy, Lewis still made his family a priority. He took the time to listen, ask thoughtful questions, got to know you on a deeper level, and found quiet ways to show you he cared.

He loved a good bike ride, walk, traveling, tennis, the arts, funky dancing, and was a voracious reader and writer.

Samoa News management and staff send love and condolences to his wife, Eletise Matagi Wolman; children: Tavie, Jessica, Homer, Iopa; and his sisters Nicky and Ruth; and his 14 grandchildren: Emelia, Ma'ata, Lewy, Fatu, Eden, AJ, Tali, Tunoa, Sina, Vao, Fin, Moana, Murphy, Talia; and many nieces and nephews.

His celebration of life will be held on Tuesday, August 4, 2026, at the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints meetinghouse on 4655 Table Mesa Dr., Boulder, CO.

item.title: Obituaries for July 29
item.description:
Francis Lonkay Agustin, 85, of Pahala died July 20 at The Queen’s Medical Center in Honolulu. Born in Kapapala, he was a retired seed planter for the former Ka‘u Sugar Co. and member of Holy Rosary Catholic Church. Visitation 8:30-10 a.m., Saturday, Aug. 8, at Holy Rosary Catholic Church in Pahala. Mass at 10 a.m. Burial to follow at Naalehu County Cemetery. Casual attire; flowers welcome. Survived by wife, Marilou Agustin of Pahala; daughters, Loretta (Jimmy) Mariano and Rose (Craig) Agustin of Kealakekua; sons, Salvador Agustin and Jonathan Agustin of Pahala; brothers, Herman (Liwani) Agustin Sr., of Philippines, Pedelino (Lydia) Agustin of Pahala and Emilio Agustin Sr. of Pepeekeo; sister, Rose Agustin of Ewa Beach, Oahu; seven grandchildren and six great-grandchildren; nieces, nephews and cousins. Arrangements by Dodo Mortuary.

The post Obituaries for July 29 appeared first on Hawaii Tribune-Herald.

item.title: American Samoa scholars travel to Washington, D.C.
item.description:
Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — American Samoa’s NOAA Hollings and EPP/MSI Scholars traveled to Washington, D.C. to present their summer research at the NOAA Education Science and Education Symposium.

Talofa Fe’a (EPP/MSI) presented her work on understanding Ciguatera in American Samoa for which she received the award for the outstanding oral presentation, while Ella Ashford (Hollings) presented about using ROVs and photogrammetry to monitor coral reefs. 

Congratulations to both of you!

item.title: Economic development a key priority for Administration
item.description:
By 
Samoa News staff
reporters@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — Governor Pulaalii Nikolao Pula noted that the proposed budget for Fiscal Year 2027 reflects an Administration focusing on building a stronger, more resilient, and self-sustaining economy rather than just achieving immediate fiscal stabilization. He acknowledged that while challenges persist, the progress made over the last two fiscal years lays a solid foundation for continued growth and responsible governance.

As reported earlier by Samoa News, the proposed budget totals $789.3 million, representing a 2 percent decrease from the FY 2026 budget.

Samoa News notes that two points should be acknowledged about the FY 2027 budget submission. First, the governor’s ceiling set forth in his call letter was for $133 million, while the budget documents are now reporting $137.9 million; and, second, it’s unknown if either ceiling amounts account for the government’s debt service or other pledged revenues — these are amounts that ASG are obligated pay before government operations are funded.

The Governor emphasized that American Samoa's long-term success relies on maintaining sound fiscal discipline and making strategic investments aimed at strengthening the economy, modernizing government operations, and enhancing the quality of life for residents. He points out that federal pandemic assistance programs are winding down, making the Territory increasingly depend more on sustainable local revenues, prudent financial management, and policies that foster private-sector investment and economic diversification.

The Pula and Pulu Administration says that it is committed to ensuring structurally balanced budgets, which are supported by realistic revenue projections and responsible spending controls, which safeguards essential public services while safeguarding the Territory's long-term financial health and minimizing reliance on one-time funding sources.

At the heart of its efforts is economic development — a key priority for the Administration. As such, the governor says it is focusing on investments in critical infrastructure — such as transportation, ports, broadband connectivity, energy resilience, water systems, healthcare facilities, and public safety — looking to create new commercial opportunities, enhance government services, and boost American Samoa's competitiveness within the Pacific region.

The Administration is touting several transformational initiatives that it believes are poised to positively impact the Territory’s economic outlook. They are:

The Google Le Vasa submarine cable project, once completed, will significantly enhance broadband capacity and improve digital connectivity for businesses, educational institutions, healthcare providers, and government entities.

The implementation of the Port Development Vision that aims to modernize maritime infrastructure, enhance regional trade, boost cargo efficiency, and position Pago Pago Harbor as a more competitive logistics hub in the Pacific.

The Administration states that it also recognizes that long-term prosperity hinges on strengthening the Territory’s workforce. As such, investments in education, vocational training, healthcare recruitment and retention, as well as workforce development programs, will continue to prepare American Samoa’s residents for emerging job opportunities while decreasing reliance on imported labor in critical sectors.

Enhancing government efficiency is another vital goal, the Administration is promoting — especially in how it handles its money. Ongoing modernization of financial management systems, tax administration, procurement processes, customs operations, and digital government services, it says will improve transparency, enhance accountability, boost revenue collection, and provide improved public services while gradually reducing administrative costs.

It is also addressing its longstanding financial obligations. The Administration states that it is committed to collaborating with stakeholders to strengthen the Government Employees' Retirement Fund, responsibly manage government liabilities, and enhance the Territory's long-term financial standing without compromising current public services.

Continuing, the Administration acknowledges that federal partnerships will remain crucial for American Samoa’s future. The Administration says it will actively pursue competitive federal grants, infrastructure funding opportunities, and strategic partnerships that leverage local investments. It will also advocate for equitable federal policies that address the unique geographic and economic challenges facing America's southernmost territory.

Despite uncertainties stemming from global economic conditions, inflationary pressures, fuel prices, supply chain disruptions, and geopolitical developments, the Administration says that American Samoa enters Fiscal Year 2027 from a position of improved fiscal stability compared to recent years. This is a result of conservative budgeting, disciplined financial management, and continued economic development investments that have fortified the Territory's capability to tackle future challenges while seizing emerging opportunities.

The governor characterized the Fiscal Year 2027 Budget as transcending mere annual financial planning; it embodies a long-term pledge to responsible governance, economic resilience, and sustainable growth.

For the upcoming budget review, the governor states that the Administration remains devoted to collaborating with the Fono, the Judiciary, federal partners, village leaders, and the residents of American Samoa. Though differences in perspective are natural within a representative governance framework, the shared responsibility to enhance the quality of life for those we serve remains unchanged.

Local News
Tags: 
ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT

item.title: Senate unanimously confirms Roy J.D. Hall Jr. as Administrative Law Judge
item.description:
By 
Asi Andrew Fa'asau
reporters@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — Roy J.D. Hall, Jr., one of American Samoa’s most senior attorneys, was unanimously confirmed yesterday to serve as the Territory’s Administrative Law Judge. All 17 senators present for the Senate vote supported his appointment, reflecting broad legislative confidence in his legal experience and long service to the community.

Hall becomes the fourth person to hold the position, which oversees administrative hearings, adjudicates regulatory disputes, and ensures due‑process protections across government agencies.

During his confirmation hearing before the Senate Judiciary Committee, chaired by Senator Leatuaolevao Asifoa, veteran attorney Roy J.D. Hall Jr. delivered a reflective and heartfelt summary of his 52 years in the legal profession — a career spanning private practice, government service, legislative counsel, and judicial roles. Hall said he was grateful for “another opportunity to serve the people and government of American Samoa.”

He thanked Governor Pulaali‘i Nikolao Pula for nominating him and opened his remarks by praising God for sustaining him throughout his decades of service.

Hall devoted a portion of his testimony to acknowledging the people who shaped his life and career. He paid tribute to his late parents — Roy J.D. Hall Sr., a retired U.S. Navy veteran from Pago Pago, and Toaiva Ofoia of Vaitogi — crediting them for instilling in him a strong Christian faith, respect for elders, and pride in his Samoan heritage.

He also recognized the support of his siblings, recalling their encouragement during his childhood health challenges and later educational pursuits. Hall thanked his wife Jacklyn and their children for standing by him through “the long days and hours” of private practice and his years as Deputy Attorney General. Their love, he said, gave him the strength to pursue his lifelong dream of becoming an attorney.

Hall’s résumé reflects one of the most extensive public‑service records in the Territory. He served two terms in the House of Representatives, worked as a District Court Judge Pro Tempore, chaired both the American Samoa Visitors Bureau and the Board of Directors of ASTCA, and provided legal counsel to the Senate under then‑President Lolo Letalu Moliga.

He also served as counsel to the Senate Select Investigative Committee (SSIC) and has spent the last four years as Deputy Attorney General, handling complex legal matters on behalf of the government.

In the Senate chamber, Hall pledged that if confirmed, his rulings would be grounded in fairness, integrity, and respect for constitutional rights.

“My goal as an attorney was to ensure that all parties receive their constitutional right to due process and a fair and impartial trial,” Hall said. “If confirmed to serve as Administrative Law Judge, I will apply these same principles of fairness, integrity, constitutional and judicial due process to everyone who comes before the Administrative Law Court.”

Committee Chair Leatuaolevao noted that senators were well aware of Hall’s long service and said his credentials were unquestioned. Leatuaolevao briefly asked Hall for his opinion on the unsettled issue of director confirmations, referencing the Fono’s position that all directors should be submitted for confirmation versus the Governor’s stance that directors of line agencies under his office need not be confirmed. After posing the question, Leatuaolevao added that Hall did not need to answer.

Senator Gaoteote Palaie Tofau also spoke highly of Hall’s experience and expressed full support for his nomination. Gaoteote noted that some directors appear at hearings represented by attorneys, and asked Hall why this occurs. Hall explained that while confirmation hearings do not require legal counsel, a subpoena does, and in those cases the Attorney General’s Office appears with the witness.

Senator Muagututi‘a Tauoa said he had no doubts about Hall’s qualifications but offered fatherly advice. As a son of Samoa, he said, Hall should be able to address district leaders in Samoan when appearing before the Senate. He also urged Hall to be fair, treat everyone equally, and avoid discrimination.

Senate President Tuaolo Manaia Fruean remarked that Hall and former Governor Togiola T.A. Tulafono are now the Territory’s most senior attorneys. He revealed that the Senate had been considering Hall for the role of Senate Legal Counsel, following the departure of Senate Attorney Mitzie Jessop‑Ta‘afua to the Retirement Fund Office. Tuaolo joked that perhaps the Governor, hearing of those plans, moved quickly to appoint Hall as Administrative Law Judge.

Tuaolo acknowledged Senator Muagututi‘a’s advice about speaking Samoan, noting that Hall may find English more natural in legal settings because it is the language of the courts.

Hall succeeds Marie Alailima, who has served as Administrative Law Judge since 2007.

Hall becomes the fourth person to hold the position, which oversees administrative hearings, adjudicates regulatory disputes, and ensures due‑process protections across government agencies.
During his confirmation hearing before the Senate Judiciary Committee, chaired by Senator Leatuaolevao Asifoa, veteran attorney Roy J.D. Hall Jr. delivered a reflective and heartfelt summary of his 52 years in the legal profession — a career spanning private practice, government service, legislative counsel, and judicial roles. item.title: Trump admin’s proposed prediction market rule faces public pushback
item.description:
WASHINGTON — Lawmakers, Native American tribes, consumer advocates and others are voicing strong opposition to the Trump administration’s plans to regulate sports and other wagering in the booming prediction market industry, according to a review of public comments available on Monday. The comments representing a spectrum of views are in response to last month’s proposal from the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission that would set moral boundaries for some prediction markets — which allow users to place yes/no wagers on such things as sports, elections, economic outcomes and Wall Street indices, among other events.

item.source:markdown:

Donald Wayne Amaral, 74, of Hilo died July 22 at home. Born in Hilo, he was a master mason and member of Heritage Faith Church, serving an usher, groundskeeper and deacon. Visitation 5-5:30 p.m. Friday, Aug. 7, at Heritage Faith Church in Hilo. Memorial service at 5:30 p.m. Food and fellowship following the service. Aloha attire. Survived by sister, Joyce (William) Tabar of Keaau; brothers, Thomas Zapra and Francine Zapra of Oahu; daughters, Georgiana (Ron) Washington of Tennessee, Maureen (Kyle) Kerbaugh of Oahu and Kainoa (Jack) Springs of North Carolina; son, Ivan (Malia) Louis of Kailua-Kona; 14 grandchildren, great-grandchildren; nieces and nephews. Arrangements by Dodo Mortuary.

item.title: Appeals court upholds blocks on Trump order restricting mail voting
item.description:
WASHINGTON — An appeals court on Saturday upheld a lower-court ruling blocking key parts of an executive order from President Donald Trump to restrict voting by mail, the latest setback to his efforts to wrest control over elections as Republicans try to protect slim congressional majorities in an unfriendly political environment.

item.description: The Houthis enacted a maritime blockade against Saudi Arabian-linked ships and ports, dealing another blow to shipping in the Middle East. Transits in the Strait of Hormuz were down this week compared to the previous week as the U.S. struck Iran for the 13th straight day. London-based Lloyd’s List Intelligence tracked 78 transits between July 13 and Sunday compared to 174 between July 6-12. Both east and westbound transits took a hit with 44 eastbound transits between July 13 and Sunday compared to 101 the prior week. Westbound transits dropped from 73 to 34 in the same period. item.title: American Samoa to welcome "Chasing Yesterday" Team with island hospitality
item.description:
UTULEI, AMERICAN SAMOA — This morning, American Samoa is poised to welcome five extraordinary endurance runners from the internationally recognized “Chasing Yesterday” team as they arrive to pursue an ambitious endurance challenge while inspiring people around the world through perseverance, determination, and community.

The Chasing Yesterday team is attempting a world-first marathon challenge across the International Date Line to raise funds and awareness for Nacoa (National Association for Children of Alcoholics). The team is reportedly completing a marathon in Samoa, then traveling "back in time" to American Samoa — to run a second marathon on the technically previous day.

Rather than taking time to rest after their flight, the team will head directly from Pago Pago International Airport to Veterans Memorial Stadium in Utulei, where they will begin running laps around the track in pursuit of their goal.

For SPW Fitness and the local organizing team, however, it is about much more than setting a record. It is about showing visitors what makes American Samoa special.

"We want these athletes to leave with more than a finish time," said SPW Fitness owner Michael McDonald. "We want them to remember the people they met, the encouragement they received, and the genuine hospitality that defines our islands."

Community members of all ages and fitness levels are invited to join the runners throughout the day. Whether someone chooses to run one lap, one mile, or simply stop by to cheer, every show of support will help create an unforgettable experience for the visiting athletes.

The event is open to everyone.

"We're not asking people to run 42 kilometers," McDonald said. "We're simply asking people to come out and be part of something positive. Walk a lap. Run a lap. Cheer from the sidelines. Encourage these runners and show them the spirit of American Samoa."

The visit also provides an opportunity to promote healthy lifestyles and community involvement, demonstrating that fitness is about encouraging one another regardless of age or ability.

American Samoa has built a reputation for welcoming visitors with warmth, generosity, and family values. Organizers hope tomorrow's event reflects those same qualities.

"We often talk about Samoan hospitality," McDonald added. "Tomorrow we have the opportunity to put that hospitality on full display."

EVENT DETAILS

Date: Friday, July 24, 2026

Arrival: 8:05 a.m.

Location: Veterans Memorial Stadium

Activity: The Chasing Yesterday team will run directly from the airport to the stadium and continue their run immediately.

Community Invitation: Everyone is welcome to participate. Run, walk, cheer, or simply stop by to encourage the runners.

SPW Fitness, Make American Samoa Healthy Again, and the BEST TOURS teams extend their sincere appreciation to all volunteers, supporters, and community members who will help make this event a memorable experience for both the visiting athletes and American Samoa.

Together, let's show them why American Samoa is unlike anywhere else in the world.

item.title: “Stand with the Moana” demonstration calls on feds to listen to Samoan voices
item.description:
By 
Asi Andrew Fa'asau
andrew@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — A different approach to expressing strong opposition to deep‑sea mining in American Samoa’s waters took shape along the Utulei shoreline last Thursday, where youth, elders, educators, conservation advocates, government employees, fishermen, families, and community leaders gathered in a unified demonstration of respect for the ocean and shared concern over proposed federal deep-sea mining leases.

The demonstration, called “Stand with the Moana” (Stand with the Ocean), was organized by Finafinau, a nonprofit organization dedicated to cultivating leadership — especially among youth — in environmental advocacy, conservation, and community resilience.

Attended by nearly 80 community members, Stand with the Moana was intentionally designed as a peaceful demonstration rooted in Pacific values, rather than a rally centered on speeches or politics. Participants gathered along the Utulei shoreline dressed in blue, offered flowers to the ocean, observed a moment of silence, and reflected on the moana’s role as a source of life, culture, identity, and the wellbeing of future generations.

According to Dr. Sabrina Suluai‑Mahuka, Executive Director of Finafinau, the demonstration brought together many different parts of the community.

Of the participants who signed in, 22 were youth under 18, showing that young people are playing an important role in discussions about caring for the ocean. People from government offices, schools, environmental groups, community organizations, local businesses, Indigenous advocates, and local residents all took part, reflecting wide support for the event.

Dr. Suluai‑Mahuka said the event was held on Manu‘a Flag Day to honor Manu‘a, since any harm from deep‑sea mining would likely affect Manu‘a first. She also explained that Stand with the Moana was organized because the federal government has not listened to Indigenous Samoan voices and is moving too quickly with its plan to lease offshore areas for deep‑sea mining.

She emphasized that the gathering was not a protest against technology or innovation. Instead, it was meant to show Pacific values of caring for the ocean and to affirm that Indigenous communities should have a real say in decisions about their ancestral waters.

Unlike many public demonstrations, Stand with the Moana did not include many speeches. Dr. Suluai‑Mahuka gave a short welcome, shared a brief reflection on the cultural importance of the ocean, and invited everyone to pause for a moment before placing flowers into the sea. The event ended with time for conversation, media interviews, and group photos.

"The purpose wasn't to convince people through a microphone," Suluai-Mahuka said. "It was to create a space where people could reconnect with why this ocean matters in the first place."

When asked if the American Samoa Government should do more to inform people about deep‑sea mining, she said awareness alone isn’t enough. The issue needs real, meaningful involvement from the public — not just messages or announcements.

She said the government has a chance to show real leadership by setting up an open, community‑focused process that keeps people informed as the federal leasing moves ahead.

"This is a generational decision," Dr. Suluai‑Mahuka said. "It shouldn't be limited to a handful of people having ‘a seat at the table’. The people of American Samoa deserve to have their voices heard too.

"People shouldn't have to piece together information from federal websites or social media to understand what's happening in our own waters," she said. "The community deserves regular public briefings on where BOEM is in the process, what decisions are coming next, and what opportunities exist for public input."

Suluai‑Mahuka said the public should be able to see and discuss any proposed lease conditions before anything is finalized.

If there are proposed conditions attached to a lease, the people should know what those are. Those documents shouldn't only be discussed behind closed doors. They should be presented publicly, explained in plain language, and open to community feedback."

She also said public education must give people the full picture.

"If public funds are being used for outreach, that outreach should help people understand both the potential benefits and the documented risks of deep-sea mining. An informed community is one that has access to all the facts and it should be cited facts, not half truths or watered down information."

In the end, Dr. Suluai‑Mahuka said the government’s job isn’t just to join federal discussions, but to make sure the community is informed and genuinely involved.

"Our elected leaders don't just have a responsibility to sit at the table," she said. "They have a responsibility to bring the people with them. Decisions that could affect our ocean for generations should never be made without the people who will live with those consequences."

Reflecting on the demonstration, organizers said what mattered most wasn’t how many people showed up, but the wide range of community members who chose to stand together.

"We saw children standing beside elders, government employees beside nonprofit leaders, fishermen beside teachers," said Uisaina Collins, a Finafinau board member and Stand with the Moana organizer. "Many people came simply because they love the ocean. That reminded us this conversation is bigger than politics. It's about the place we all call home."

She also pointed out how meaningful the international support was throughout the day, with people sharing photos and messages from beaches, coastlines, rivers, and communities across the Pacific and beyond.

"American Samoa may be geographically small, but this demonstrates that we are not standing alone," she said. "Communities across Oceania and Indigenous nations around the world understand that the health of the ocean is a shared responsibility."

As the federal leasing process moves forward, organizers say Stand with the Moana is just one part of a much longer community conversation.

"Our hope has never been simply to oppose something," Suluai-Mahuka said. "We stand today because our children do not deserve an apology. They deserve an inheritance. An ocean that is still alive. A culture that is still thriving. And a generation that chose to protect both.

The deep‑sea mining controversy began with the Federal Executive Order expanding federal authority to accelerate domestic mineral supply chains, including seabed minerals, and instructed agencies to identify potential offshore areas for exploration. This is the policy foundation BOEM used when it began evaluating Pacific federal waters — including those around American Samoa — for possible deep‑sea mining leases.

"In just a few months, we've gone from an Executive Order directing agencies to expedite offshore critical mineral development to a proposed leasing process that could determine the future of our ocean for decades," said Dr. Sabrina Suluai-Mahuka. "Last Thursday's Stand with the Moana demonstration was an opportunity for our community to pause, gather peacefully, and remind ourselves and decision-makers that before this ocean is viewed as a resource, it is our home."

She emphasized that the event welcomed anyone regardless of political affiliation or organizational membership. A demonstration grounded in reflection.

On May 20, 2025, the U.S. Department of the Interior announced it was initiating an evaluation for a potential offshore mineral lease sale near American Samoa — the first such action in more than 30 years.

This announcement triggered BOEM’s subsequent notices and ultimately led to the territory’s town hall meeting in July last year. The majority of speakers voiced strong opposition to any exploration or extraction of minerals from the ocean floor in waters near American Samoa. Concerns ranged from environmental risks to the potential disruption of cultural and marine ecosystems.

Several individuals and local groups and organizations have voiced their strong opposition to the proposed deep-sea mining project.

Local and national environmental groups have voiced disappointment that the Trump Administration is moving forward with plans to open federal waters near American Samoa to deep‑sea mining.

On Friday, BOEM released a proposed notice outlining two 20‑year leases for mineral extraction on portions of the Pacific Ocean floor. Each lease area carries a minimum bid of $3 million.

"We must reject the false narrative that deep-sea mining is inevitable or that financial royalties are worth sacrificing our future," said Dr. Sabrina Suluai-Mahuka.

“We are talking about permanent, generational consequences to our ocean and our cultural heritage. Our elected officials have immense power to stop this, and we demand they use it immediately. Also, folks need to understand that this idea of national security is also a false narrative. They need to check out verified  reports like Deep Deception which has hundreds of citations to combat this fallacy”.

Dr. Suluai Mahuka said the Governor has the explicit authority to reject rushed timelines and demand comprehensive, multi-year ecological impact data before any lease proceeds.

GOVERNMENT STATEMENT

In a statement issued Friday, Governor Pulaali‘i Nikolao Pula acknowledged BOEM's release of the proposed deep‑sea mining lease sale in federal waters near American Samoa.

The Governor noted that the Department of the Interior (DOI) and BOEM have maintained steady, transparent communication with the American Samoa Government (ASG) throughout the process, including timely updates on the Proposed Lease Notice.

“This is an opportunity for our community to provide informed input,” Governor Pulaali’i added. “Should BOEM ultimately decide to move forward with a lease sale, I remain steadfast in my position that any such development must be fully transparent, responsible, science-based, and carefully managed to protect our environment, safeguard our vital tuna fisheries and cultural heritage, and deliver meaningful, tangible benefits for the people of American Samoa.”

CONGRESSWOMAN AMATA

In a statement issued Friday, Congresswoman Uifa’atali Amata reaffirmed her opposition to seabed mining in waters near American Samoa. She emphasized that her stance has remained consistent and unchanged, despite recent assumptions or characterizations suggesting otherwise.

Uifa’atali also made clear that no one speaks on her behalf regarding this issue — not Republicans, not Democrats, and not any outside groups. Her position, she said, is her own and has been firmly maintained.

“This is my seventh public statement on this issue, because of its importance, and because various posts, comments, or statements sometimes say they describe my position – they do not. I was clear from the beginning, first that I stand with the people and then with further statements of opposition as we learned more. I submitted opposition comments to the Interior Department, and in the congressional record speaking out at congressional committee hearings. I remain opposed and consistent,” said Congresswoman Uifaatali Amata.

36TH GENERAL ASSEMBLY OF THE CCCAS

At the opening of the 36th General Assembly of the Congregational Christian Church of American Samoa this week, the keynote speaker urged the church to take a clear and courageous stand against deep‑sea mining.

Addressing more than 600 delegates and church members packed into the Ua Taunuu Church at Kanana‑fou on Monday morning, Rev. Dr. Upolu Luma Vaai — Vice Chancellor and Professor of Theology & Ethics at Pasifika Communities University in Suva, Fiji — said there are still far too many unanswered questions surrounding proposals to explore and extract minerals from waters near American Samoa.

He said it is both timely and appropriate for the church to speak out, emphasizing its responsibility to safeguard the ocean, the environment, and future generations.

His keynote paper, delivered in Samoan, drew directly from the General Assembly’s theme, “God Takes Residence in Creation,” emphasizing the theological and ethical imperative to protect the natural world.

The demonstration, called “Stand with the Moana” (Stand with the Ocean), was organized by Finafinau, a nonprofit organization dedicated to cultivating leadership — especially among youth — in environmental advocacy, conservation, and community resilience.
Attended by nearly 80 community members, Stand with the Moana was intentionally designed as a peaceful demonstration rooted in Pacific values, rather than a rally centered on speeches or politics. Participants gathered along the Utulei shoreline dressed in blue, offered flowers to the ocean, observed a moment of silence, and reflected on the moana’s role as a source of life, culture, identity, and the wellbeing of future generations.
According to Dr. Sabrina Suluai‑Mahuka, Executive Director of Finafinau, the demonstration brought together many different parts of the community.
Of the participants who signed in, 22 were youth under 18, showing that young people are playing an important role in discussions about caring for the ocean. People from government offices, schools, environmental groups, community organizations, local businesses, Indigenous advocates, and local residents all took part, reflecting wide support for the event.
Dr. Suluai‑Mahuka said the event was held on Manu‘a Flag Day to honor Manu‘a, since any harm from deep‑sea mining would likely affect Manu‘a first. She also explained that Stand with the Moana was organized because the federal government has not listened to Indigenous Samoan voices and is moving too quickly with its plan to lease offshore areas for deep‑sea mining.
She emphasized that the gathering was not a protest against technology or innovation. Instead, it was meant to show Pacific values of caring for the ocean and to affirm that Indigenous communities should have a real say in decisions about their ancestral waters.
Unlike many public demonstrations, Stand with the Moana did not include many speeches. Dr. Suluai‑Mahuka gave a short welcome, shared a brief reflection on the cultural importance of the ocean, and invited everyone to pause for a moment before placing flowers into the sea. The event ended with time for conversation, media interviews, and group photos.
"The purpose wasn't to convince people through a microphone," Suluai-Mahuka said. "It was to create a space where people could reconnect with why this ocean matters in the first place."
When asked if the American Samoa Government should do more to inform people about deep‑sea mining, she said awareness alone isn’t enough. The issue needs real, meaningful involvement from the public — not just messages or announcements.
She said the government has a chance to show real leadership by setting up an open, community‑focused process that keeps people informed as the federal leasing moves ahead.
"This is a generational decision," Dr. Suluai‑Mahuka said. "It shouldn't be limited to a handful of people having ‘a seat at the table’. The people of American Samoa deserve to have their voices heard too.
"People shouldn't have to piece together information from federal websites or social media to understand what's happening in our own waters," she said. "The community deserves regular public briefings on where BOEM is in the process, what decisions are coming next, and what opportunities exist for public input."
Suluai‑Mahuka said the public should be able to see and discuss any proposed lease conditions before anything is finalized.
If there are proposed conditions attached to a lease, the people should know what those are. Those documents shouldn't only be discussed behind closed doors. They should be presented publicly, explained in plain language, and open to community feedback."
She also said public education must give people the full picture.
"If public funds are being used for outreach, that outreach should help people understand both the potential benefits and the documented risks of deep-sea mining. An informed community is one that has access to all the facts and it should be cited facts, not half truths or watered down information."
In the end, Dr. Suluai‑Mahuka said the government’s job isn’t just to join federal discussions, but to make sure the community is informed and genuinely involved.
"Our elected leaders don't just have a responsibility to sit at the table," she said. "They have a responsibility to bring the people with them. Decisions that could affect our ocean for generations should never be made without the people who will live with those consequences."
Reflecting on the demonstration, organizers said what mattered most wasn’t how many people showed up, but the wide range of community members who chose to stand together.
"We saw children standing beside elders, government employees beside nonprofit leaders, fishermen beside teachers," said Uisaina Collins, a Finafinau board member and Stand with the Moana organizer. "Many people came simply because they love the ocean. That reminded us this conversation is bigger than politics. It's about the place we all call home."
She also pointed out how meaningful the international support was throughout the day, with people sharing photos and messages from beaches, coastlines, rivers, and communities across the Pacific and beyond.
"American Samoa may be geographically small, but this demonstrates that we are not standing alone," she said. "Communities across Oceania and Indigenous nations around the world understand that the health of the ocean is a shared responsibility."
As the federal leasing process moves forward, organizers say Stand with the Moana is just one part of a much longer community conversation.
"Our hope has never been simply to oppose something," Suluai-Mahuka said. "We stand today because our children do not deserve an apology. They deserve an inheritance. An ocean that is still alive. A culture that is still thriving. And a generation that chose to protect both.
The deep‑sea mining controversy began with the Federal Executive Order expanding federal authority to accelerate domestic mineral supply chains, including seabed minerals, and instructed agencies to identify potential offshore areas for exploration. This is the policy foundation BOEM used when it began evaluating Pacific federal waters — including those around American Samoa — for possible deep‑sea mining leases.
"In just a few months, we've gone from an Executive Order directing agencies to expedite offshore critical mineral development to a proposed leasing process that could determine the future of our ocean for decades," said Dr. Sabrina Suluai-Mahuka. "Last Thursday's Stand with the Moana demonstration was an opportunity for our community to pause, gather peacefully, and remind ourselves and decision-makers that before this ocean is viewed as a resource, it is our home."
She emphasized that the event welcomed anyone regardless of political affiliation or organizational membership. A demonstration grounded in reflection.
On May 20, 2025, the U.S. Department of the Interior announced it was initiating an evaluation for a potential offshore mineral lease sale near American Samoa — the first such action in more than 30 years.
This announcement triggered BOEM’s subsequent notices and ultimately led to the territory’s town hall meeting in July last year. The majority of speakers voiced strong opposition to any exploration or extraction of minerals from the ocean floor in waters near American Samoa. Concerns ranged from environmental risks to the potential disruption of cultural and marine ecosystems.
Several individuals and local groups and organizations have voiced their strong opposition to the proposed deep-sea mining project.
Local and national environmental groups have voiced disappointment that the Trump Administration is moving forward with plans to open federal waters near American Samoa to deep‑sea mining.
On Friday, BOEM released a proposed notice outlining two 20‑year leases for mineral extraction on portions of the Pacific Ocean floor. Each lease area carries a minimum bid of $3 million.
"We must reject the false narrative that deep-sea mining is inevitable or that financial royalties are worth sacrificing our future," said Dr. Sabrina Suluai-Mahuka.
“We are talking about permanent, generational consequences to our ocean and our cultural heritage. Our elected officials have immense power to stop this, and we demand they use it immediately. Also, folks need to understand that this idea of national security is also a false narrative. They need to check out verified reports like Deep Deception which has hundreds of citations to combat this fallacy”.
Dr. Suluai Mahuka said the Governor has the explicit authority to reject rushed timelines and demand comprehensive, multi-year ecological impact data before any lease proceeds.
**GOVERNMENT STATEMENT**
In a statement issued Friday, Governor Pulaali‘i Nikolao Pula acknowledged BOEM's release of the proposed deep‑sea mining lease sale in federal waters near American Samoa.
The Governor noted that the Department of the Interior (DOI) and BOEM have maintained steady, transparent communication with the American Samoa Government (ASG) throughout the process, including timely updates on the Proposed Lease Notice.
“This is an opportunity for our community to provide informed input,” Governor Pulaali’i added. “Should BOEM ultimately decide to move forward with a lease sale, I remain steadfast in my position that any such development must be fully transparent, responsible, science-based, and carefully managed to protect our environment, safeguard our vital tuna fisheries and cultural heritage, and deliver meaningful, tangible benefits for the people of American Samoa.”
**CONGRESSWOMAN AMATA**
In a statement issued Friday, Congresswoman Uifa’atali Amata reaffirmed her opposition to seabed mining in waters near American Samoa. She emphasized that her stance has remained consistent and unchanged, despite recent assumptions or characterizations suggesting otherwise.
Uifa’atali also made clear that no one speaks on her behalf regarding this issue — not Republicans, not Democrats, and not any outside groups. Her position, she said, is her own and has been firmly maintained.
“This is my seventh public statement on this issue, because of its importance, and because various posts, comments, or statements sometimes say they describe my position – they do not. I was clear from the beginning, first that I stand with the people and then with further statements of opposition as we learned more. I submitted opposition comments to the Interior Department, and in the congressional record speaking out at congressional committee hearings. I remain opposed and consistent,” said Congresswoman Uifaatali Amata.
**36TH GENERAL ASSEMBLY OF THE CCCAS**
At the opening of the 36th General Assembly of the Congregational Christian Church of American Samoa this week, the keynote speaker urged the church to take a clear and courageous stand against deep‑sea mining.
Addressing more than 600 delegates and church members packed into the Ua Taunuu Church at Kanana‑fou on Monday morning, Rev. Dr. Upolu Luma Vaai — Vice Chancellor and Professor of Theology & Ethics at Pasifika Communities University in Suva, Fiji — said there are still far too many unanswered questions surrounding proposals to explore and extract minerals from waters near American Samoa.
He said it is both timely and appropriate for the church to speak out, emphasizing its responsibility to safeguard the ocean, the environment, and future generations.
His keynote paper, delivered in Samoan, drew directly from the General Assembly’s theme, “God Takes Residence in Creation,” emphasizing the theological and ethical imperative to protect the natural world.

item.title: VIDEO: Decommissioned USS Mobile Bay, USS Peleliu Sunk in RIMPAC Drills
item.description: This story has been updated with additional information that was released after publication. Mobile Bay was sunk July 11 and Peleliu was sunk July 17 by forces from the U.S. and partner nations in sinking exercises, according to a U.S. Navy news release published Wednesday. Both ships were sunk in waters 15,000 feet deep, more than 50 nautical miles off the northern coast of the island

item.title: DOH attended a Pediatric Behavioral Summit in Las Vegas this month
item.description:
Representatives from American Samoa DOH Behavioral Health Services Division and Maternal and Child Health Program attended a Pediatric Behavioral Summit in Las Vegas this month.

It was a 2-day summit packed with speakers and professionals who shared their vast experiences working with children and adolescents with mental and behavioral issues.

Team Amerika Samoa pictured are: Dr. Peni Biukoto, AD Talalupelele Sunia-Fiso, RN Patricia Masaniai, and PD Ipuniuesea Eliapo-Unutoa.

item.title: US judge sets June 2027 trial date for Venezuela’s Maduro
item.description:
NEW YORK — A judge on Wednesday set a June 1, 2027, trial date for ousted Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores on U.S. drug trafficking charges, while a defense lawyer vowed to seek dismissal of the case on the grounds that Maduro is immune from prosecution as the head of a sovereign state. Maduro and his wife, wearing beige prison garb, appeared during a hearing lasting about 20 minutes in Manhattan federal court before U.S. District Judge Alvin Hellerstein in one of the most consequential criminal cases in recent U.S. history. U.S. commandos captured Maduro, 63, and Flores, 69, at their heavily guarded home in Caracas during a January 3 nighttime military raid ordered by President Donald Trump. They were brought to New York, where they previously had been indicted on charges of using their leadership positions in the oil-rich South American country to facilitate cocaine shipments. They have pleaded not guilty.

The post US judge sets June 2027 trial date for Venezuela’s Maduro appeared first on Hawaii Tribune-Herald.
item.source:markdown:
NEW YORK — A judge on Wednesday set a June 1, 2027, trial date for ousted Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores on U.S. drug trafficking charges, while a defense lawyer vowed to seek dismissal of the case on the grounds that Maduro is immune from prosecution as the head of a sovereign state. Maduro and his wife, wearing beige prison garb, appeared during a hearing lasting about 20 minutes in Manhattan federal court before U.S. District Judge Alvin Hellerstein in one of the most consequential criminal cases in recent U.S. history. U.S. commandos captured Maduro, 63, and Flores, 69, at their heavily guarded home in Caracas during a January 3 nighttime military raid ordered by President Donald Trump. item.title: Amphib USS Tripoli Wraps 6-month Indo-Pacific, Middle East Patrol
item.description: Big deck amphibious ship USS Tripoli (LHA-7), lead ship of the Tripoli Amphibious Ready Group, wrapped up on Wednesday a six-month patrol that took the group to the Indo-Pacific and Middle East. Tripoli pulled into White Beach Naval Facility, Okinawa, on Wednesday to offload elements of the 31st Marine Expeditionary Unit. Along with the embarked 31st MEU, the Tripoli ARG included Tripoli, amphibious transport dock USS New Orleans (LPD-18) and amphibious dock landing ship USS Rushmore (LSD-47). Tripoli, forward deployed to Japan, departed in mid-January in preparation for the annual U.S. Marine Corps – Japan Ground Self-Defense Force exercise Iron

item.title: ASCC Psychology Class supports Fagaima fire victims
item.description:
By 
James Kneubuhl, ASCC Press Officer

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA —  A fire last month in Fagaima resulted in four of the village’s families losing their homes. In response to the needs of the fire victims, students in two sections of the American Samoa Community College (ASCC) summer class Introduction to Psychology (PSY 150) recently organized a donation of household goods and personal items to help the four affected families during their period of transition into new living spaces.

Under the leadership of instructor Mrs. Tala Ropeti-Leo, the 28 students in PSY 150 sections 1 and 2 presented the donation to representatives from each family during a presentation held at ASCC on Thursday, July 9th..

Mrs. Ropeti-Leo shared that her classes — comprising two sections of PSY 150 — organized themselves into groups of four, which each group planning how to fundraise and which items they would get. “Some students sewed pillowcases and made the pillows themselves,” she said, “while others did walkathons and pledges so they could make purchases.” By the end of the fundraising period the students had more than enough goods to distribute evenly between the four families.

“There was such an abundance of clothes, shoes, blankets, pillows, beddings, food items as well as baby items and basic hygiene items,” she recalled.

At the July 9th ceremony, PSY 150 students Vise Feagaiga and Fuarosa Molesi acted as class representatives and presented the donations to the four families. Faaitaita Faaifoaso spoke on behalf of the families, who also had representatives present.

Since she began teaching Introduction to Psychology at ASCC little over ten years ago, Mrs. Ropeti-Leo has always had her students engage in a community service project each spring, summer and fall semester.

She gives them the option to work individually, but says they usually choose to work as a group, sometimes on projects that utilize fundraising, and other times on activities that only require their time, such as volunteering at the summer school programs as reading tutors or doing beach cleanups. During the current summer semester, when she told her students about the fire in Fagaima that consumed the four households, they immediately voted to support these families’ during their recovery.

A project that supports the community in some way becomes in itself a valuable learning experience, Mrs. Ropeti-Leo emphasized. “Aside from donating time, effort, money or items in these projects,” she explained, “students have the opportunity to improve communication, organizational and leadership skills, as well as their ability to express ideas and be creative on how to come up with the donations of their choice. In the process of getting their donations together, students also advance in their engagement and collaboration skills.

“Some of my students who rarely ask questions or speak up during class discussion are more vocal and more enthusiastic when they work in these projects. As an instructor, I see a lot more harmony and collaboration amongst students as they organize a service for their community.”

When asked how community service relates to Psychology, Mrs. Ropeti-Leo shared some insights based on her long experience in linking the subject with real-life experience.

“One of the core course learning outcomes for PSY 150 is that students gain an understanding of themselves and others through the application of theories in the field of Psychology,” she said. “Through these projects, students become active members of their community and have a lasting positive impact on society by providing a service to those in need.

“The act of giving actually triggers psychological benefits by activating brain regions associated with reward and social connection, which is something we discuss in class. Students learn that by making donations to the fire victims, they play a role in mitigating the victims' trauma, which ranges from emotional shock to post-traumatic stress and sleep deprivation.”

With public service projects having become a regular component of her PSY 150 classes, Mrs. Ropeti-Leo pointed out how the “service” often involves the public itself.

“This project was made possible by my amazing 28 students and the support of the community,” she explained. “For all who supported my students and I, whether it was giving money, clothes, shoes, or food items, we thank you so much for helping us make this possible.

“In doing these community service projects, I hope the students learn to work well with each other and enjoy giving back to the community, but also that they foster a sense of responsibility to their community, their people, and those around them, especially those in need.”

For more information on educational activities and opportunities at ASCC, visit the College’s website at www.amsamoa.edu.

item.title: Obituaries for July 22
item.description:
Jared Bobby Kaipolani Abong, 44, of Hilo died June 26 at Hilo Benioff Medical Center. Born in Hilo, he worked for a moving company, was a member of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Keaukaha Ward and loved music, fishing and boogie boarding. Private services at a later date. Survived by father, Robert James Abong of Hilo; mother, Edwina Uilani Kukahiko of Hilo; sisters, Crystal Lena Abong of Hilo, Shantel (Ryan) Root of Oregon, Shila Abong of Hilo and Terrilyn Abong of Papaikou; brother, Miles Kukahiko of California; nieces, nephews, cousins, aunts and uncles. Arrangements by Dodo Mortuary.

The post Obituaries for July 22 appeared first on Hawaii Tribune-Herald.

After a 33-year Army career after which he was director of the supplemental nutrition assistance program (SNAP) for the Western Regional Office, FNS/USDA — retired Army Command Sgt. Major Charles Tobin is returning home to American Samoa. 

“As my career in public service ends, I reflect on the immeasurable pride of being part of something bigger than myself,” he told Samoa News in a recent email. Thank you for a life of service to your country and your community!

item.title: Swains Island faipule once again asking Fono for consideration in FY2027 budget
item.description:
Most important is the need for reliable transportation to the island
By 
Samoa News staff
reporters@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — The Swains Island Representative Alexander Jennings is again asking the Fono, as they prepare for the 2027 Budget Hearings, for consideration regarding the continued transportation hardship faced by Swains Island. In particular, he highlights that Swains Island residents have endured decades of unreliable access to essential services, emergency support, and basic mobility, and points to the lack of budgeted assistance from the ASG for the last twenty years — “less than one-half percent” of the annual budget.

Jennings’ request was made in an email to his fellow House representatives, dated July 20, 2027. The Fono is currently in recess until July 27, 2026, when the 4th Regular Session will once again resume its business.

For the FY 2027 budget, he is requesting Fono support for his proposal of $300,000 for Swains Island Transportation in the FY 2027 Budget.

This funding level, according to Jennings will secure:

  • Quarterly Manu’atele trips to Swains Island;
  • Quarterly MV Mataliki trips through partnership with Tokelau; and,
  • At least three MV Lady Samoa trips during the 2027 calendar year through partnership with Samoa.

The Swains faipule states that “this modest but essential investment will finally provide Swains Island with predictable, government‑supported transportation — a basic service that has been lacking for far too long.”

He further notes that a near fatal incident in their recent visit to the Swains Island on May 13, 2026 — the first since 2023 for a required security inspection — forced them to rely on foreign governments — Samoa and Tokelau — for transportation assistance. The incident occurred when a 12-foot rubber dinghy used to transport personnel and supplies ashore capsized in the channel throwing three overboard, narrowly avoiding a serious disaster.

Jennings explains that “no written explanation can fully convey Swains Island’s dependence on the MV Manu‘atele and the LCU- Uila o le Sami — both acquired with federal funds and both essential to our survival. Unlike Tutuila, Aunu‘u, and the Manu‘a islands, Swains Island has no harbor, no wharf, and no alternative means of safe access. Our only entry point is a narrow channel carved by nature, not infrastructure.”

He continues that without the MV Manu‘atele, they have been reduced to 2 fishing boats and a 12-foot dinghy for transportation.

Faipule Jennings has communicated directly with the Director of Port Administration Barney Sene, with copies sent to Gov. Pulaali’i Nikolao Pula, Congresswoman Uifaatali Aumua Amata and the US Department of the Interior to highlight the severity of the situation and limited supported currently available.

Notably, in one of his email responses to the Port Admin director, Jennings explains that his request in purchasing the LCU- Uila o le Sami in its current condition was not as a private individual — “a distinction that has repeatedly been misapplied to deny Swains Island access to government assistance. Every request I make in my official capacity as the Swains Island Delegate, is for the benefit of the people of Swains Island.”

He points to the lack of reliable transportation as the reason “our people were forced to evacuate our homeland”. And, goes on to point out that “according to the U.S. Department of the Interior, Swains Island is legally entitled to the same federal funding opportunities as Tutuila and Manu‘a. Yet in more than twenty years of service, I have witnessed a consistent and systemic failure to recognize Swains Island as an equal beneficiary under federal law.

“This disparity was most glaring during the distribution of the $1.4 billion in ARPA funding — now in its final phase — from which Swains Island received no assistance whatsoever, despite numerous requests. The same inequitable treatment now appears to be occurring with respect to this federally funded LCU.

“The Swains Island Community Economic Development Corporation is a nonprofit organization incorporated under American Samoa law to serve Swains Island and its community of U.S. Nationals. Under territorial laws, the people of Swains Island are recognized as persons of Samoan ancestry, native Samoans, permanent residents, bona fide residents, and lineal descendants of the current titleholder, with heritable rights to the island.

“Like all lands in American Samoa, Swains Island is privately held — under Samoan custom for Tutuila and Manu‘a, and under U.S. citizenship lineage for Swains.

“To ensure equal treatment of all U.S. Nationals, the framers of our Constitution — our forefathers, together with the United States — explicitly extended to Swains Island the same privileges and protections granted under the Deeds of Cession for Tutuila and Manu‘a. This constitutional mandate is not discretionary. It is binding. Transferring the LCU to the Swains Island Community Organization is fully consistent with this mandate and directly supports the safety, access, and legal rights of our people.

“Despite these constitutional guarantees, Swains Island has also been denied equitable access to local funding for more than two decades. For example, out of the $800+ million FY2026 budget, Swains Island received an assistance of only $45,000—less than one‑half of one percent—for transportation.

“According to your Department, this amount is insufficient even to fund a single trip with the MV Manu'atele to the island.  Subsequently, Governor Pula graciously granted my request to scale down our 101 year Fag Day Anniversary of being part of American Samoa, in order to accommodate a much needed security inspection since our last visit to Swains Island in 2023. 

“Sadly, this visit was accomplished by the use of two small fishing boats with a 12' dinghy to take people and supplies to shore, because no other vessel was available.

“A review of at least the past twenty years will show the same pattern of exclusion,” Jennings states.

The Swains Island faipule was responding to an email he received from Director of Port Admin Sene on June 4, 2026 that reviewed his request to purchase the LCU- Uila o le Sami. Sene wrote:

Unfortunately, the LCU "Uila o le Sami":

  1. It was acquired with federal funds, which brings up some unique challenges.
  2. If sold today, the depreciation — factoring in its current lifespan versus its expected 20-year lifespan — would need assessment and consideration.
  3. We must follow a formal ASG "Asset" disposal process, which requires the following:
    • a.  The Survey Board surveys the vessel to determine its value and remaining useful life.
    • b.  If the item can be salvaged or repaired before the auction, what would be the cost, or what is the minimum surveyed cost for the auction?  
    • c.  This process takes a minimum of 90 days from start to finish.

Items #1 and #2 above puts your entire request on full stop.

My suggestion is:

1.  New Vessel:  Look for another vessel (new or existing) in this location or in the states where you can purchase and operate as a private vessel

2.  Funds for Repair:  Help us find funding to repair and restore the vessel so the Port Administration can operate or charter it out (not lease, give up, or hand over the use or operating of, to a private entity or person) for the proposed use.

Most important is the need for reliable transportation to the island

By
Samoa News staff
reporters@samoanews.com
_Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA —_ The Swains Island Representative Alexander Jennings is again asking the Fono, as they prepare for the 2027 Budget Hearings, for consideration regarding the continued transportation hardship faced by Swains Island. In particular, he highlights that Swains Island residents have endured decades of unreliable access to essential services, emergency support, and basic mobility, and points to the lack of budgeted assistance from the ASG for the last twenty years — “less than one-half percent” of the annual budget.
Jennings’ request was made in an email to his fellow House representatives, dated July 20, 2027. The Fono is currently in recess until July 27, 2026, when the 4th Regular Session will once again resume its business.
For the FY 2027 budget, he is requesting Fono support for his proposal of $300,000 for Swains Island Transportation in the FY 2027 Budget.
This funding level, according to Jennings will secure:
- Quarterly Manu’atele trips to Swains Island; - Quarterly MV Mataliki trips through partnership with Tokelau; and, - At least three MV Lady Samoa trips during the 2027 calendar year through partnership with Samoa.
The Swains faipule states that “this modest but essential investment will finally provide Swains Island with predictable, government‑supported transportation — a basic service that has been lacking for far too long.”
He further notes that a near fatal incident in their recent visit to the Swains Island on May 13, 2026 — the first since 2023 for a required security inspection — forced them to rely on foreign governments — Samoa and Tokelau — for transportation assistance. The incident occurred when a 12-foot rubber dinghy used to transport personnel and supplies ashore capsized in the channel throwing three overboard, narrowly avoiding a serious disaster.
Jennings explains that “no written explanation can fully convey Swains Island’s dependence on the MV Manu‘atele and the LCU- Uila o le Sami — both acquired with federal funds and both essential to our survival. Unlike Tutuila, Aunu‘u, and the Manu‘a islands, Swains Island has no harbor, no wharf, and no alternative means of safe access. Our only entry point is a narrow channel carved by nature, not infrastructure.”
He continues that without the MV Manu‘atele, they have been reduced to 2 fishing boats and a 12-foot dinghy for transportation.
Faipule Jennings has communicated directly with the Director of Port Administration Barney Sene, with copies sent to Gov. Pulaali’i Nikolao Pula, Congresswoman Uifaatali Aumua Amata and the US Department of the Interior to highlight the severity of the situation and limited supported currently available.
Notably, in one of his email responses to the Port Admin director, Jennings explains that his request in purchasing the LCU- Uila o le Sami in its current condition was not as a private individual — “a distinction that has repeatedly been misapplied to deny Swains Island access to government assistance. Every request I make in my official capacity as the Swains Island Delegate, is for the benefit of the people of Swains Island.”
He points to the lack of reliable transportation as the reason “our people were forced to evacuate our homeland”. And, goes on to point out that “according to the U.S. Department of the Interior, Swains Island is legally entitled to the same federal funding opportunities as Tutuila and Manu‘a. Yet in more than twenty years of service, I have witnessed a consistent and systemic failure to recognize Swains Island as an equal beneficiary under federal law.
“This disparity was most glaring during the distribution of the $1.4 billion in ARPA funding — now in its final phase — from which Swains Island received no assistance whatsoever, despite numerous requests. The same inequitable treatment now appears to be occurring with respect to this federally funded LCU.
“The Swains Island Community Economic Development Corporation is a nonprofit organization incorporated under American Samoa law to serve Swains Island and its community of U.S. Nationals.
